title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics

epigraph.quote: Retailers fail when they mistake store count for capital efficiency; the winners own the brand and lease the metal.
epigraph.author: Unit-economics principle in branded jewellery

web_blocks.html: Titan's retail footprint reached 3,603 stores across 440+ Indian towns by FY26 [2][3]. That network spans Tanishq, Mia, CaratLane, Titan World, Fastrack, Helios, Titan Eye+, and Taneira [2]. Titan scales capital-heavy gold showrooms without starving ROCE through a three-tier franchise model: L1, L2, and L3 [16]. Franchise partners supply local real estate and store capital while Titan controls brand and inventory rules.

web_blocks.caption: Tanishq Store Economics: L1 (COCO) vs. L2 (COFO) vs. L3 (FOFO) Architecture
rows: Flagship metros, Zoya ateliers, international launches; highest gross margin, lowest capital turn [16].
Primary Tier-1/Tier-2 expansion engine; Titan retains inventory control while shedding lease/payroll capex [16].
Owned by franchisee (buys outright from Titan)
Tier-2/Tier-3 rapid penetration; highest ROCE for Titan, near-zero balance-sheet inventory drag [16].
web_blocks.takeaway: By shifting incremental store openings toward L2 and L3 franchisees, Titan captures wholesale/retail brand economics while keeping store real-estate and staff overhead off its fixed-cost base.

web_blocks.html: Gold-on-Lease (GML) & Hedging Mechanics: Titan avoids speculative gold exposure by leasing bullion via Gold Metal Loans [14][18]. Banks lend physical gold at ~1.5%–3.5% lease rates for 180 days, and Titan fixes the price only when a customer buys [14][18]. That natural hedge neutralizes spot gold swings on leased stock. Residual unleased inventory is hedged through commodity futures and spot contracts [14]. Finally, customer advances like the Golden Harvest Scheme provide low-cost working capital and lock in future purchases.

Manufacturing & Karigar Ecosystem: Titan operates modern plants in Hosur, Pantnagar, and Sikkim, alongside dedicated Karigar Centres [2][17]. These centres house master artisans in safe, formal workshops instead of fragmented sweatshops [17]. Vertical integration cuts gold wastage, enforces diamond quality, and speeds up store replenishment [17].

web_blocks.title: The Hidden Leverage in Working Capital: Borrowings vs. Gold-on-Lease
paragraphs: Notice how Screener's Balance Sheet shows Borrowings climbing from ₹5,638 crore in FY21 to ₹30,621 crore in FY26 (and ₹27,638 crore in Sep 2026), while Finance Costs rose from ₹203 crore to ₹1,180 crore (and ₹1,521 crore TTM) [1]. Under Ind AS, Gold-on-Lease liabilities and lease obligations sit inside Borrowings/Other Liabilities, inflating as gold prices surge and as Titan consolidates Damas and CaratLane. While GML is operationally hedged, rising lease rates and higher inventory days (222 days in FY26 vs. 176 days in FY24) mean interest coverage and inventory velocity must be monitored closely [1].

book_paragraphs: To understand why Titan earns a 20.5% return on capital employed in a business that sells heavy physical gold, you and I have to look beneath the showroom carpet. If Titan owned every square foot of real estate and paid cash up front for every gram of gold sitting in its 3,603 stores, its balance sheet would drown in working capital.

Instead, Titan engineered a three-part capital-efficiency machine. First, it splits its store expansion into L1 company-owned flagships, L2 partner-operated stores where Titan owns the gold, and L3 full-franchise stores in smaller towns where the local partner funds both the showroom and the inventory. That lets Tanishq plant flags in 440+ towns while keeping fixed-asset capex remarkably light—just ₹877 crore in FY26 against ₹87,584 crore in sales.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: THE ₹100 REVENUE WATERFALL
book_callouts.text: When we break down ₹100 of Titan's FY26 sales, ₹90.46 goes straight out the door for bullion, diamonds, karigar making, and operating overhead. Only ₹9.54 remains as Operating EBITDA, and ₹5.79 reaches Net Profit. In a thin-percentage-margin business, survival depends on inventory turns and cash conversion—which is why FY26's ₹5,590 crore operating cash flow and ₹4,713 crore free cash flow matter far more than any single quarter's headline sales spike.

book_subsections.title: Gold-on-Lease, Karigar Parks & The Borrowing Question
paragraphs: The second pillar is Gold-on-Lease, also known as Gold Metal Loans. Rather than tying up cash to buy bullion months before a wedding season, Titan borrows physical gold from bullion banks at a modest lease fee and prices the metal only on the day a customer swipes their card at the register. That turns gold price volatility from an existential gamble into a hedged pass-through.

The third pillar is the Karigar Park network—clean, mechanized artisan hubs near Hosur and other centres that eliminated middlemen, cut gold wastage, and standardized studded craftsmanship. Yet there is a watch-item you and I cannot ignore: consolidated borrowings rose from ₹5,638 crore in FY21 to ₹30,621 crore in FY26 (₹27,638 crore by September 2026), pushing TTM interest costs to ₹1,521 crore. Much of that reflects gold-on-lease liabilities swollen by record gold prices and the Damas acquisition, but 222 inventory days in FY26 leaves less room for sloppy demand.
